title: Dosing hens with Flubenvet wormer
subtitle: The UK licensed wormer for laying hens and how to administer it correctly.
excerpt: Flubenvet is the only licensed wormer for laying hens in the UK. It kills all the major species of roundworm and the gizzard worm Gizzardworm in one seven-day course, and there is no egg-withdrawal period at the licensed dose. Here is how to calculate the dose, mix it into feed, and manage the treatment course.
sourceNotes: Elanco UK, Flubenvet 1% product information and prescribing data (2023). AHDB Poultry, worm control in backyard flocks. RSPCA, worming guidance for small flock keepers.

glossaryTerms.definition: The active ingredient in Flubenvet. A benzimidazole anthelmintic that works by disrupting energy metabolism in nematode worms. Effective against Ascaridia galli, Capillaria species, and Heterakis gallinarum in poultry.

content.text: at 1% concentration and is supplied as a premix powder. At the licensed dose (60 g per 20 kg of feed, giving 60 ppm in the total ration), no egg withdrawal period applies. If the dose rate is exceeded, an egg withdrawal period of seven days applies. This distinction matters for home flock keepers who eat and sell from the same birds.
The licensed dose for small flocks is: 6 g of Flubenvet 1% powder per 1 kg of feed. Lay hens eat approximately 120 to 130 g of feed per bird per day. To treat 10 hens for 7 days:
Daily feed for 10 hens: 10 x 125 g = 1.25 kg.
Total feed for 7 days: 1.25 x 7 = 8.75 kg.
Flubenvet needed: 8.75 kg x 6 g/kg = 52.5 g.
Mix the total dose into the total feed batch, or weigh each daily ration and add the proportional powder each morning.
Mix the powder thoroughly into the feed. Uneven mixing means some birds receive too little and others too much. Work the powder in with a gloved hand or use a feed mixer.
Remove all other feed sources during the seven-day course. Free-range birds that can find additional feed outdoors may not receive a full dose.
Continue medicated feed for the full seven days. Do not shorten the course even if birds look well.

Most small flock keepers treat twice a year: once in spring and once in autumn, when worm burdens are typically highest. Birds in permanent runs on the same ground year-round may need more frequent treatment. A worm egg count from a faecal sample (sent to a vetlab) gives a more accurate picture of the actual burden and avoids unnecessary use of anthelmintics.
